content: The use of oral contraceptives has been associated with several serious medical conditions, including thrombophlebitis, arterial thromboembolism, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, cerebral hemorrhage, cerebral thrombosis, hypertension, gallbladder disease, and hepatic adenomas or benign liver tumors. Evidence also suggests a potential link between oral contraceptive use and mesenteric thrombosis as well as retinal thrombosis, though further confirmatory studies are required. Adverse reactions that are believed to be drug-related and have been reported in patients using oral contraceptives include nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal symptoms (such as abdominal cramps and bloating), breakthrough bleeding, spotting, changes in menstrual flow, amenorrhea, temporary infertility after discontinuation of treatment, edema, and melasma (which may persist). Breast-related changes such as tenderness, enlargement, and secretion have also been noted. Other reported effects include changes in weight (either increase or decrease), alterations in cervical erosion and secretion, diminished lactation when administered immediately postpartum, cholestatic jaundice, migraines, allergic rashes, mental depression, reduced carbohydrate tolerance, vaginal candidiasis, changes in corneal curvature (steepening), and intolerance to contact lenses. Additional adverse reactions reported in users of oral contraceptives, though their association has not been definitively confirmed or refuted, include congenital anomalies, premenstrual syndrome, cataracts, optic neuritis, changes in appetite, cystitis-like syndrome, headache, nervousness, dizziness, hirsutism, loss of scalp hair, erythema multiforme, erythema nodosum, hemorrhagic eruption, vaginitis, porphyria, impaired renal function, hemolytic uremic syndrome, Budd-Chiari syndrome, acne, changes in libido, colitis, sickle-cell disease, cerebral-vascular disease with mitral valve prolapse, and lupus-like syndromes. Postmarketing experience for the oral contraceptive product Cryselle is not documented in the FDA package insert. Drug interactions have been observed with oral contraceptives. Concomitant use of rifampin has been associated with reduced efficacy of oral contraceptives and an increased incidence of breakthrough bleeding and menstrual irregularities. Similar, though less pronounced, interactions have been suggested with barbiturates, phenylbutazone, phenytoin sodium, and possibly with griseofulvin, ampicillin, and tetracyclines. Oral contraceptives may also affect laboratory test results. They can increase prothrombin and clotting factors VII, VIII, IX, and X, while decreasing antithrombin III levels and increasing norepinephrine-induced platelet aggregability. Thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) levels may rise, leading to increased circulating total thyroid hormone levels, as measured by protein-bound iodine (PBI), T4 by column, or radioimmunoassay. Free T3 resin uptake is decreased due to elevated TBG, but free T4 concentrations remain unchanged. Other serum-binding proteins, including sex hormone-binding globulins, may also be elevated, resulting in increased levels of total circulating sex steroids and corticosteroids, though free or biologically active levels remain unaffected. Triglyceride levels may increase, glucose tolerance may decrease, and serum folate levels may be depressed, which could be clinically significant if a woman becomes pregnant shortly after discontinuing oral contraceptives. Regarding specific populations, oral contraceptives are classified as Pregnancy Category X by the FDA, indicating that they should not be used during pregnancy. There is no FDA guidance on their use during labor and delivery, in geriatric populations, or in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids have been detected in the breast milk of nursing mothers, and adverse effects on the child, such as jaundice and breast enlargement, have been reported. Oral contraceptives may also interfere with lactation by reducing the quantity and quality of breast milk. Nursing mothers are advised to use alternative forms of contraception until they have completely weaned their child. The safety and efficacy of oral contraceptives have been established in women of reproductive age, including postpubertal adolescents under the age of 16. However, their use before menarche is not indicated. There is no FDA guidance on the use of oral contraceptives in immunocompromised patients or specific gender or racial populations. Oral contraceptives are administered orally. There is no information in the FDA package insert for Cryselle regarding drug monitoring or IV compatibility. In cases of overdose, serious adverse effects have not been reported following acute ingestion of large doses of oral contraceptives by young children. Overdose may cause nausea, and withdrawal bleeding may occur in females. The pharmacology of norgestrel/ethinyl estradiol is not extensively detailed in the drug label. The primary mechanism of action of combination oral contraceptives is the suppression of gonadotropins, primarily through the inhibition of ovulation. Additional effects include changes in cervical mucus, which increase the difficulty of sperm entry into the uterus, and alterations in the endometrium, which reduce the likelihood of implantation.
